hints: Look inside the pale round nucleus of cell D and cell E in Fig. 1.1 and count how many small, very dark round spots you can see in each.
walkthrough:
Seeing Interphase Clearly**
Both D and E show large round nuclei with diffuse chromatin and a clear nuclear envelope, so both are in interphase. In interphase the nucleolus, the dark spot where ribosomal RNA is made, is visible.

Counting The Dark Spots**
If you count the dense black dots, D clearly shows two separate nucleoli while E shows only one single nucleolus. That is the visible difference.
Final answer: Cell D has two nucleoli in its nucleus and cell E has one nucleolus.

hints: Compare the appearance of the stained chromatin in A, B and C - in which cells is it still a tangled mass inside an intact nucleus, and in which cell has it formed separate thick structures moving apart?
Remember that chromosomes get shorter, thicker and more deeply stained as prophase progresses, while anaphase is recognised by sister chromatids separating toward opposite poles.

Use the degree of condensation to order A and B - the looser, more thread-like mass is earlier prophase and the thicker, more distinct coiled chromosomes are later prophase - and use the V-shapes at opposite ends to name C.
walkthrough:
Reading Prophase From Chromosome Shape**
In prophase chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes while the nucleolus disappears. Cell A still shows thin, thread-like chromatin just starting to condense, so it is early to mid prophase. Cell B shows much thicker, shorter, more intensely stained and clearly coiled chromosomes, so it is further on, mid to late prophase.

Spotting Anaphase**
Cell C shows two sets of V-shaped sister chromatids, now called daughter chromosomes, pulled to opposite poles of the cell by spindle fibres. That separation to poles is diagnostic of anaphase, not prophase or metaphase where chromosomes are still together.
Final answer: cell A = early / mid prophase; cell B = mid / late prophase; cell C = anaphase.

hints: Cells F and G have just finished division with a new cell plate, so think about which stage of mitosis restores two separate interphase-like nuclei just before cytokinesis starts.
Focus on what must happen at each pole to the clustered daughter chromosomes, their surrounding membrane and the spindle for the nuclei to return to working condition.
walkthrough:
Placing Telophase Before Cytokinesis**
Cytokinesis with a cell plate in plants follows telophase. By telophase, anaphase separation is complete, so you have two groups of daughter chromosomes, one cluster at each pole of the old cell.

Rebuilding Working Nuclei**
Around each cluster the nuclear envelope reforms to make two separate nuclei. Inside, the chromosomes uncoil and become long and diffuse again as chromatin, the nucleolus reappears, and the spindle breaks down. Cells F and G then divide cytoplasm to give the two new daughter cells.

Final answer: In telophase: daughter chromosomes arrive in two groups at opposite poles; nuclear envelope reassembles around each group; nucleolus reappears; chromosomes decondense to chromatin; spindle disassembles. Any two.
